section.title: The Flight to Egypt
section.sectionRationale: The remnant left after Gedaliah's murder asks Jeremiah to seek God's guidance and vows in advance to obey whatever he says, pleasant or unpleasant. When the answer comes, stay in the land, do not fear Babylon, do not go to Egypt, they reject it outright, accuse Jeremiah and Baruch of manipulation, and drag the whole remnant, prophet and scribe included, down into Egypt anyway.
section.thesis: A remnant that swears in advance to obey whatever God says proves, the moment the answer is unwelcome, that its request for guidance was never sincere, and drags God's own prophet into the very disobedience he warned against.
section.frameNote: Four scenes: the remnant seeks guidance and vows total obedience; God's answer through Jeremiah, stay in the land and do not fear, do not go to Egypt; the remnant's outright rejection of that word and forced march to Egypt; and a sign at Tahpanhes that Babylon will follow them even there.

units.label: The remnant seeks guidance, vowing obedience
units.note: a request made in advance of the answer

verses.text: Then all the commanders of the forces, along with Johanan son of Kareah, Jezaniah son of Hoshaiah, and all the people from the least to the greatest, approached
Jeremiah the prophet and said, “May our petition come before you; pray to the LORD your God on behalf of this entire remnant. For few of us remain of the many, as you can see with your own eyes.
Pray that the LORD your God will tell us the way we should walk and the thing we should do.”
“I have heard you,” replied Jeremiah the prophet. “I will surely pray to the LORD your God as you request, and I will tell you everything that the LORD answers; I will not withhold a word from you.”
Then they said to Jeremiah, “May the LORD be a true and faithful witness against us if we do not act upon every word that the LORD your God sends you to tell us.
Whether it is pleasant or unpleasant, we will obey the voice of the LORD our God to whom we are sending you, so that it may go well with us, for we will obey the voice of the LORD our God!”

units.label: God's answer: stay, do not fear, do not go to Egypt
units.note: life and blessing offered, if they will only remain

verses.text: After ten days the word of the LORD came to Jeremiah,
and he summoned Johanan son of Kareah, all the commanders of the forces who were with him, and all the people from the least to the greatest.
Jeremiah told them, “Thus says the LORD, the God of Israel, to whom you sent me to present your petition:
‘If you will indeed stay in this land, then I will build you up and not tear you down; I will plant you and not uproot you, for I will relent of the disaster I have brought upon you.
Do not be afraid of the king of Babylon, whom you now fear; do not be afraid of him, declares the LORD, for I am with you to save you and deliver you from him.
And I will show you compassion, and he will have compassion on you and restore you to your own land.’
But if you say, ‘We will not stay in this land,’ and you thus disobey the voice of the LORD your God,
and if you say, ‘No, but we will go to the land of Egypt and live there, where we will not see war or hear the sound of the {{shofar|ram's horn}} or hunger for bread,’
then hear the word of the LORD, O remnant of Judah! This is what the LORD of Hosts, the God of Israel, says: ‘If you are determined to go to Egypt and reside there,
then the sword you fear will overtake you there, and the famine you dread will follow on your heels into Egypt, and you will die there.
So all who resolve to go to Egypt to reside there will die by sword and famine and plague. Not one of them will survive or escape the disaster I will bring upon them.’

For this is what the LORD of Hosts, the God of Israel, says: ‘Just as My anger and wrath were poured out on the residents of Jerusalem, so will My wrath be poured out on you if you go to Egypt. You will become an object of cursing and horror, of vilification and disgrace, and you will never see this place again.’
The LORD has told you, O remnant of Judah, ‘Do not go to Egypt.’ Know for sure that I have warned you today!
For you have deceived yourselves by sending me to the LORD your God, saying, ‘Pray to the LORD our God on our behalf, and as for all that the LORD our God says, tell it to us and we will do it.’
For I have told you today, but you have not obeyed the voice of the LORD your God in all He has sent me to tell you.
Now therefore, know for sure that by sword and famine and plague you will die in the place where you desire to go to reside.”

units.label: The remnant defies the word, drags Jeremiah to Egypt
units.note: rejecting the very word they vowed to obey

verses.text: When Jeremiah had finished telling all the people all the words of the LORD their God, everything that the LORD had sent him to say,

Azariah son of Hoshaiah, Johanan son of Kareah, and all the arrogant men said to Jeremiah, “You are {{kazab|lying}}! The LORD our God has not sent you to say, ‘You must not go to Egypt to reside there.’
Rather, Baruch son of Neriah is inciting you against us to deliver us into the hands of the Chaldeans, so that they may put us to death or exile us to Babylon!”
So Johanan son of Kareah and all the commanders of the forces disobeyed the command of the LORD to stay in the land of Judah.
Instead, Johanan son of Kareah and all the commanders of the forces took the whole remnant of Judah, those who had returned to the land of Judah from all the nations to which they had been scattered,

the men, the women, the children, the king's daughters, and everyone whom Nebuzaradan captain of the guard had allowed to remain with Gedaliah son of Ahikam, the son of Shaphan, as well as Jeremiah the prophet and Baruch son of Neriah.
So they entered the land of Egypt because they did not obey the voice of the LORD, and they went as far as Tahpanhes.

units.label: A sign at Tahpanhes: Nebuchadnezzar will come
units.note: no refuge lies outside God's word

verses.text: Then the word of the LORD came to Jeremiah at Tahpanhes:
“In the sight of the Jews, pick up some large stones and bury them in the clay of the brick pavement at the entrance to Pharaoh's palace at Tahpanhes.

Then tell them that this is what the LORD of Hosts, the God of Israel, says: ‘I will send for My servant Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon, and I will set his throne over these stones that I have embedded, and he will spread his royal pavilion over them.
He will come and strike down the land of Egypt, bringing death to those destined for death, captivity to those destined for captivity, and the sword to those destined for the sword.

I will kindle a fire in the temples of the gods of Egypt, and Nebuchadnezzar will burn those temples and take their gods as captives. So he will wrap himself with the land of Egypt as a shepherd wraps himself in his garment, and he will depart from there unscathed.
He will demolish the sacred pillars of the temple of the sun in the land of Egypt, and he will burn down the temples of the gods of Egypt.’”

shofar.gloss: A ram's horn trumpet, sounded to warn of approaching war. The remnant's stated hope in fleeing to Egypt is never again hearing this sound, imagining safety outside the land where God had actually promised to protect them.

kazab.gloss: To lie, to speak falsely. The arrogant men accuse Jeremiah of exactly this, lying, immediately after solemnly vowing to obey whatever true word the LORD would give them, the plainest possible proof that the vow was never sincere.

basic.context: After Gedaliah's murder, the frightened remnant asks Jeremiah to seek God's guidance and swears in advance to obey it completely, whether the answer is pleasant or unpleasant. Ten days later Jeremiah delivers God's clear answer: stay in the land, do not fear Babylon, and above all do not go to Egypt, for those who flee there will die by the very sword and famine they are trying to escape. The remnant's leaders immediately accuse Jeremiah of lying and Baruch of manipulating him, then force the entire remnant, including Jeremiah and Baruch themselves, down into Egypt. At Tahpanhes, God gives a sign that Babylon's king will follow them even there.
basic.hermeneutics: The narrative exposes a universal pattern: a request for guidance made while already resolved on a course of action is not really a request at all. Jeremiah names this exactly, you have deceived yourselves, verse 20, since the vow to obey was tested the moment the answer proved unwelcome and failed instantly. The passage does not merely record disobedience; it records self-deceived disobedience dressed up as piety.
basic.originalLanguages: The people hope in Egypt to escape the sound of the shofar, the ram's horn that signals approaching war, imagining safety where God has promised only that the sword and famine they fear will overtake them. When the answer displeases them, they accuse Jeremiah of kazab, lying, the very charge that exposes their own vow as false, since a true vow to obey cannot survive contact with an unwelcome command.
basic.typology: The remnant's flight to the very place God forbade, seeking safety in Egypt rather than trusting His presence in the land, inverts the Exodus pattern, in which God once led His people out of Egypt toward the promised land; here they flee back into Egypt against His word.
basic.christ: Where Israel's history began with God bringing His people out of Egypt, this remnant reverses that pattern entirely, running back into Egypt out of unbelief rather than trusting the God who promised to build and plant them in the land. Christ, the greater and obedient Son, is Himself carried into Egypt as an infant and brought out again, Matthew 2:15 quoting Hosea 11:1, fulfilling in perfect obedience the pattern Israel and this remnant kept failing to walk in faith.
basic.god: God offers real mercy and even relents of disaster if only the remnant will trust Him and remain, verses 10 to 12, showing His discipline is never merely punitive. Yet He is also entirely truthful in warning what unbelief will cost, and He does not remove the consequences of a choice made against clear revealed guidance, even though He continues to speak to and provide for His people, Jeremiah included, even in their disobedience.
basic.crossReferences: Hosea 11:1 and Matthew 2:15 tie Egypt to both Israel's history and Christ's own infancy. Deuteronomy 17:16 warns the king himself against returning the people to Egypt. James 1:22 calls hearers to be doers of the word, not merely hearers who deceive themselves. Isaiah 30:1-3 similarly condemns seeking refuge in Egypt against God's counsel.
basic.oneStory: A remnant vows to obey God completely, then breaks that vow the instant His answer proves unwelcome, dragging His own prophet down into the very disobedience he warned against. This is the persistent shape of the human heart across the whole Bible, professing obedience while resolved on its own way, a pattern only undone when Christ, the truly obedient Son, walks the path of perfect trust where Israel and this remnant could not.

context.literary:
The passage is built as a three part test with a long fuse. Jeremiah 42:1 to 6 is the question and the vow, 42:7 to 22 is the answer, and 43:1 to 7 is the verdict on the people's hearts. Then 43:8 to 13 stands apart as a coda, a word given after the march has already happened. The shape is the shape of a trial: a promise made in advance, evidence produced, and a judgment that falls on the person who made the promise.

Notice how the speakers' language is turned against them. The people say 'the LORD your God' four times in 42:2 to 5 and shift to 'the LORD our God' only inside the vow of 42:6. Jeremiah's answer then quotes their words back to them, 42:20, so that their own sentences become the charge sheet. The structure of the divine answer is also careful. Verses 10 to 12 are an if clause with a promise, verses 13 to 18 are the opposite if clause with a threat, and verses 19 to 22 close with a doubled 'know for sure.' Every fear the people listed in 42:14, war, the ram's horn, hunger, is picked up in verse 16 and reversed. They meant to flee three dangers and they are told those very dangers will chase them.

Chapter 43 gives the reply in a single burst, then slows down to list who was marched off: men, women, children, the king's daughters, the prophet and his scribe. The list is deliberately full, as though the narrator wanted every name present at the scene of the disobedience. The sign act at Tahpanhes, 43:8 to 13, is the only piece of drama in the section. Stones are set in mortar where Pharaoh's door opens, and a throne is promised for a conqueror on the spot.
context.historical:
The setting is about 586 to 582 BC. Jerusalem has fallen, the Babylonian governor Gedaliah has been murdered at Mizpah by Ishmael son of Nethaniah, Jeremiah 41:1 to 3, and Johanan son of Kareah has rescued the captives and halted at Geruth Chimham, near Bethlehem, already intending to go on to Egypt, 41:17 to 18. That detail matters: the petition of chapter 42 is made by people who had their bags half packed. The Babylonians would have been expected to punish the killing of their appointee, and fear of that reprisal, not hunger or war, is what drives the flight. Second Kings 25:26 confirms that the people small and great fled to Egypt for fear of the Chaldeans.

Egypt was the natural refuge. It was the great grain basket, it was a rival of Babylon, and Judah had a long history of leaning on it for help, Isaiah 30:1 to 3 and 31:1. Pharaoh Hophra, called Apries in Greek sources, was reigning, and had probably tried to relieve Jerusalem in Zedekiah's day, Jeremiah 37:5 to 7. Tahpanhes, the place where the party stops, lay on Egypt's eastern frontier and served as a fortified border post. Soldiers and their families fleeing from Judah would have found familiar company there, which is one reason the refugees settled in communities along the delta, as chapter 44:1 lists.

The 'stones in the clay of the brick pavement' of 43:9 speak to the architecture of a border palace. The Hebrew phrase refers to a paved area at the entrance of the royal residence, the sort of platform where the king appeared. Jeremiah buries the stones at the very spot where the pharaoh's authority would be displayed, so that any Judean watching would see the claim written into the ground. Nebuchadnezzar is called 'My servant,' as in Jeremiah 25:9 and 27:6: a pagan king in the service of Israel's God.
context.canonical:
The chapter lives in a tradition about going back to Egypt that runs from the wilderness to the exile. In Numbers 14:3 to 4 Israel proposes to appoint a leader and return to Egypt, rejecting the land and the God who led them out. Nehemiah 9:17 remembers that same moment as an act of stiff necked rebellion. Deuteronomy 17:16 forbids the king to send the people back to Egypt, and 28:68 names a return in ships as the final curse. Hosea turns the tradition into prophecy: 'They will return to Egypt,' Hosea 8:13, and 'Ephraim will return to Egypt,' Hosea 9:3. In Jeremiah 42 and 43 these warnings come true in the most literal way. The people reverse the Exodus on foot.

There is an inner Jeremiah thread as well. The 'build and not tear down, plant and not uproot' of 42:10 reuses the vocabulary of Jeremiah's call, Jeremiah 1:10, and of the good figs, 24:6. Jeremiah 24:8 to 10 had already marked out the Judeans living in Egypt as the bad figs, so the present chapter fills out a verdict that Jeremiah had spoken years before. Jeremiah 18:7 to 10, the potter's principle that an announced judgment may be turned aside, stands behind the conditional form of the answer: if you stay, I relent.

The New Testament takes up the Egypt motif at the start of the gospel. In Matthew 2:13 to 15 Joseph takes the child to Egypt and brings Him back, and Matthew writes that this fulfilled 'Out of Egypt I called My Son,' Hosea 11:1. That text first described Israel, so Matthew presents Jesus as Israel reduced to one, doing what the nation and this remnant refused to do. Where the remnant went to Egypt at their own insistence and stayed to die, the Child goes at the angel's word and returns at the angel's word, Matthew 2:19 to 21.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
The chapters were shaped for a community in exile that wanted to know how the Judeans came to lose even the small remnant left after 586. Jeremiah, or the editors working with him, answers by showing the last decision point. The people had a prophet at hand, a promise of restoration, and a clear if hard command. They did not lack revelation; they lacked will.

The author also wants the reader to feel the tragedy of the prophet's position. Jeremiah promised in 42:4 that he would hold nothing back, and he kept that promise at a cost. He then watched himself be accused of serving Baruch's private agenda, and then he was carried into Egypt against his will. For exiles tempted to read their suffering as proof that the faithful were wrong, the narrative is a corrective: the person who spoke truth was swept along with those who refused it.

Finally the sign at Tahpanhes shows that God's word does not wait for people's consent. The refugees thought they had escaped Nebuchadnezzar's reach by crossing a border. Jeremiah's stones teach that no border sits outside the Lord's jurisdiction, and that a servant like Nebuchadnezzar can be sent for anywhere. Readers who had heard Jeremiah say 'stay and live' were meant to understand that the instruction had been a mercy, not a trap.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
The narrative describes what the remnant did and records what God said; it does not command believers to stay in any particular country or to treat migration as sin. The command to stay, 42:10, was addressed to a specific people at a specific moment under a specific promise about this land, and Jeremiah is not making a general rule about where God's people may live. Elsewhere Scripture shows faithful people in Egypt, such as Joseph, and God tells Jacob in Genesis 46:3 to 4 not to be afraid to go down there, because He would go with him.

What does carry over is the pattern of seeking guidance. A request for direction made after the heart has chosen is not a prayer but a request for a signature. The principle applies wherever believers consult Scripture, pastors or counsel only to confirm a decision they have already made. James 1:22 names the same trap of hearing and deceiving oneself. The chapter also shows that obedience cannot be pledged ahead of knowing the content. Verses 5 and 6 sound like perfect devotion, 'pleasant or unpleasant,' and the testing came only when the unpleasant arrived. The faithful response is to ask honestly and to be ready for the unwelcome answer.

debates.question: Was the remnant's refusal sincere unbelief or fear overwhelming good intentions?

views.label: Fear overcame real intent
views.case: The people came to Jeremiah in distress, called themselves a small remnant, and used the language of covenant witness in 42:5. Many readers see fear of Babylon as a pressure strong enough to break a sincere vow, much as the disciples fled Gethsemane after promising loyalty.

views.label: The petition was a pretext from the start
views.case: Jeremiah says in 42:20 that they had deceived themselves, and 41:17 shows they were already heading to Egypt. The accusation in 43:2 comes at once, with no pause for reflection. On this view the question was asked to gain religious cover for a settled plan.

debates.bearing: The text leans toward the second view, since Jeremiah diagnoses self-deception and the plan was in place beforehand. Yet the two views converge on the practical lesson: fear that is allowed to choose the destination will bend the instruction to fit it.

debates.question: Why does God promise compassion in verses 10 to 12 when He knew they would refuse?

views.label: The offer was genuine and conditional
views.case: Jeremiah 18:7 to 10 sets out the principle that God truly responds to repentance. The words 'if you will indeed stay' mean what they say, and the refusal in chapter 43 shows human responsibility, not a hidden plan overriding the offer.

views.label: The offer exposed what was already in their hearts
views.case: Because God knows the heart, He framed the choice so that their rejection would be public and without excuse. The answer in 42:20 to 22 reads like a verdict as well as a plea.

debates.bearing: Scripture holds both together: the offer is real and the refusal is culpable. The passage does not resolve how God's foreknowledge and human choice fit together, but it never lets either excuse the people.

study.originalLanguages:
Several Hebrew features sharpen the passage. First, the doubled forms. In 42:10 the phrase 'if you will indeed stay' joins an infinitive with the finite verb, so that the offer is emphatic: if you really dwell. The same construction opens the warnings of verses 19 and 22, 'know for sure,' literally knowing, you shall know. The offer and the threat are stated with the same force, which is part of Jeremiah's point. God means both.

Second, the 'build and plant' vocabulary. In 42:10 the verbs are the positive pair of Jeremiah 1:10, build and plant, set against the negative pair, tear down and uproot. In the call they were the shape of Jeremiah's whole commission. In this chapter the same four verbs are offered as a choice, and the people can decide which half of the commission falls on them. The verb 'relent' in the same verse is the one used in Jeremiah 18:8 for God turning from planned disaster. The word for 'compassion' in 42:12 comes from the same root as the word for womb, so it carries the sense of a mother's tenderness, and the verse promises that even Nebuchadnezzar will be moved by it.

Third, the verbs of pursuit in 42:16. The sword 'will overtake' them, and the famine 'will follow on your heels,' where the Hebrew for the second is a verb meaning to cling or stick. What they hope to leave behind is not behind them but attached. The Hebrew for 'reside' in 42:15, 42:17 and 43:2 is the verb of the foreign resident, the sojourner. They planned a temporary stay and the text treats it as taking the status of a resident alien outside the land of promise.

Fourth, 'determined' in 42:15 and 42:17 is literally 'set your faces' to enter Egypt. The same idiom is used when God sets His face against them in 44:11. Their set faces meet His.

Fifth, 'arrogant men' in 43:2 is the Hebrew for the presumptuous, the same family of word as the prophet who 'dares' to speak in God's name in Deuteronomy 18:20. The ones who accuse Jeremiah of presuming to speak are themselves labeled as presumptuous. A final small note: the Hebrew text of 42:1 names Jezaniah where the Septuagint and 43:2 have Azariah, a textual difference the BSB footnote records.

typology.fulfillment: Israel's story began with God bringing His people out of Egypt with a mighty hand, Exodus 14:13, and the Law forbade a return, Deuteronomy 17:16. The remnant walks that road backward, and Hosea 8:13 had already said they would. In Christ the pattern is redeemed rather than reversed: Jesus is taken into Egypt and called out of it, Matthew 2:15, and He leads a greater exodus for His people. The type falls short because Egypt in Jeremiah is a refuge from the wrong fear, while Egypt in Matthew is a protected stay under divine direction.

typology.type: The prophet carried into exile with the disobedient, Jeremiah 43:6
typology.fulfillment: Jeremiah and Baruch are taken along against their will, and Jeremiah keeps speaking God's word where he lands. This anticipates the faithful who suffer with a disobedient community, and ultimately the Servant who is numbered with transgressors, Isaiah 53:12, quoted of Jesus in Luke 22:37. The correspondence is that a righteous person bears the consequences of other people's rebellion and keeps proclaiming. It falls short because Jeremiah suffers alongside sinners, whereas Christ suffers in their place and for them.

typology.type: Stones laid at Pharaoh's door, Jeremiah 43:9 to 10
typology.fulfillment: The buried stones are an enacted prophecy: ordinary building material turned into the footing for a conqueror's throne. They resemble the prophet's other sign acts, such as the linen belt and the jar, and prefigure the way God stakes His claim on a place before it is seen. In the New Testament stones are used again, as the rejected stone that becomes the cornerstone, Matthew 21:42, so that what looks like a discarded or buried thing becomes the foundation of God's work. The type is limited: Tahpanhes announces judgment, while the cornerstone brings salvation.

study.christ:
The chapter leads to Christ most plainly by contrast with His own Egyptian journey. Matthew 2:13 to 15 tells of Joseph taking the child and His mother to Egypt and staying there until the death of Herod, and Matthew applies Hosea 11:1, 'Out of Egypt I called My Son.' Jeremiah 42 and 43 supply the dark background. A remnant of Israel chooses Egypt against a direct word and is told it will die there. The Son of God goes down to the same land under direction and returns at the same direction. Where they were told 'you will never see this place again,' 42:18, He is brought back to the land of Israel, Matthew 2:19 to 21. The contrast shows Christ as the faithful Israel who walks the road the remnant refused.

The second link is the pattern of the vow. The people said 'whether it is pleasant or unpleasant, we will obey,' and did not. Jesus faced a pleasant and unpleasant answer in Gethsemane, and chose as they would not: 'not as I will, but as You will,' Matthew 26:39. Hebrews 5:8 says He learned obedience from what He suffered. He is the one in whom the promise of 42:6 is finally kept.

A third link is the prophet who is falsely accused. Jeremiah brings an unwelcome word and is told 'You are lying' and 'Baruch is inciting you.' Jesus was accused of a false motive again and again, and the hearers who rejected Him said His word came from the devil, Matthew 12:24. The pattern, that people who dislike the message attack the messenger's character, finds its fullest example in Him. Hebrews 11:35 to 38 holds up those who refused release and suffered rather than silence their testimony.

A fourth link is the offer of a secure life. The promise in 42:10, 'I will build you up and not tear you down,' belongs to a God who will plant a people in the land. Christ announces the same builder's work in a new key, 'I will build My church,' Matthew 16:18. He is the one who plants a people that cannot be uprooted.

Finally, the passage holds up a warning the gospel makes sharper. If a people who refused a prophet met the sword in Egypt, the writer of Hebrews asks how they will escape who neglect so great a salvation, Hebrews 2:3. The same text cautions against twisting every detail into allegory. Tahpanhes is not a secret picture of the cross. The links rest on the way the New Testament itself uses the Egypt journey, the obedient Son, and the rejected prophet.
study.god:
The chapter first shows a God who answers prayer exactly and on time, though not on the people's schedule. He keeps Jeremiah waiting ten days, 42:7. The delay itself is instructive. The people wanted an answer fast enough to sound like their own conclusion, but the word came when God chose, and Jeremiah's quiet fidelity to that timetable is part of the lesson. God is not an oracle on call.

He is a God who wants to rebuild. The language of 42:10 to 12 is fatherly: 'I will build you up,' 'I will show you compassion.' The commission that made Jeremiah a prophet of demolition, Jeremiah 1:10, is here willing to turn into building. God would rather plant than uproot, and He says so to the very people who will not hear it. His wrath in the passage is the settled response of a patient God, not an impulse.

He is sovereign over fear. The one thing they feared, the king of Babylon, is the thing God promises to turn into an instrument of mercy: 'he will have compassion on you and restore you,' 42:12. The thing they trusted, Egypt and its border, turns out to be the place where the very danger finds them. God commands what they fear and sets what they trust in His service, and the sign at Tahpanhes shows Nebuchadnezzar as 'My servant' on Egyptian soil, 43:10.

He is truthful. He does not soften the penalty in 42:22 to make the refusal easier, and He does not retract the offer to make His point. He holds a high standard of honesty with people who are practised at lying to themselves. The phrase 'you have deceived yourselves' is a kindness as well as a charge, because it names the real trouble.

He is faithful to His servants. Jeremiah is dragged to Egypt and still receives a word there, 43:8. The God who spoke to him at Anathoth speaks to him at a pavement in a foreign border town, which echoes Psalm 139's confession that He is found even in the farthest parts. This does not remove the pain of the exile, but it answers the question of whether God is present in a place that was never meant to be visited.

For worship, the chapter calls us to pray with open hands. The right way to ask God for direction is to be ready for the unwelcome answer and to trust, as 42:11 puts it, that He is 'with you to save you and deliver you.' It also warns against bargaining for His blessing on a plan He has not endorsed.

crossReferences.note: The narrator sets up the whole chapter here. The survivors halt near Bethlehem 'in order to proceed into Egypt to escape the Chaldeans.' The plan precedes the petition, which explains why Jeremiah says in 42:20 that the people deceived themselves in sending him to pray.

The bad figs include those 'living in the land of Egypt.' This earlier vision foretold the very community formed in these chapters, so the flight is not a surprise to God. It is the fulfilment of a verdict, and it shows that the remnant in Egypt was never the future of the people.

The law of the king forbids sending the people back to Egypt, 'You are never to go back that way again.' Johanan and the commanders act as the leaders of a people who should have remembered that boundary, and they take the whole company back down the road the Lord closed.

At the edge of the land the earlier generation said, 'Let us appoint a leader and return to Egypt.' The echo is deliberate: both generations meet a hard word and choose Egypt, and both are told they will fall away from the promise they could have entered.

Isaiah condemned those who 'set out to go down to Egypt without asking My advice.' Jeremiah's remnant does ask, but ignores the reply. Isaiah says that Pharaoh's protection will become their shame, and the sign at Tahpanhes shows how.

Hosea warned that the Lord would remember Israel's iniquity and 'They will return to Egypt.' The phrase is a judgment, not a refuge. Jeremiah 43:7 narrates what Hosea spoke of, and 44 shows its outcome.

Joseph takes the child to Egypt by the angel's word and Matthew sees Hosea 11:1 fulfilled. Set beside Jeremiah, the story gives a double contrast: a people who went to Egypt unbidden and stayed to perish, and a Child who went at God's direction and came out when called.

James warns that those who hear and do not do are deceiving themselves. It is almost a commentary on Jeremiah 42:20. The remnant heard the word, said they would do it, and did not, which is the structure of self-deception James describes.

God told Jeremiah he was appointed to uproot and tear down, to build and plant. In 42:10 the building and planting half is offered to the remnant as a real possibility. The people's refusal means the prophet's work of demolition must continue in Egypt.

God calls Nebuchadnezzar 'My servant,' the same title used in 25:9 and 27:6. The remnant fled the man they feared, and God says the man is His. Their fear of Babylon was misplaced because the Babylonian king is moved by the God they ignored.

study.oneStory:
The Bible begins with a people placed in a good land under a clear word, and a recurring question follows: will they trust the word when the land looks dangerous? Adam heard it in the garden, Israel heard it at the edge of Canaan, and this remnant hears it among the ruins. In each scene fear drives people away from God's provision toward a substitute, and in each the substitute turns out to be the place of death. Jeremiah 42 and 43 is the exile's version of Numbers 14, a refusal to go forward in faith that sends a people back to Egypt.

What this passage sets up is the need for a faithful Israel. The nation has now gone the full circle: it left Egypt under Moses, entered the land, lost it, and the survivors flee back into the place they were rescued from. The old covenant history has run out of road. Jeremiah himself points beyond this when he speaks of a new covenant written on the heart, Jeremiah 31:31 to 34, a covenant that does what vows made with lips alone could not do. A vow like 42:6, however earnest, cannot keep itself.

Christ steps into that gap. Matthew's gospel opens by having Him walk the whole history of Israel in miniature: down to Egypt, out of Egypt, through water and wilderness, each time obedient where Israel was not. He bears the consequences of the people's faithlessness and offers instead a heart that obeys. Those who follow Him are given the Spirit, which is how the words 'we will obey' become true.

The end of the story answers the fear that drove the remnant. In the new creation there is no sword, no famine and no border to flee. 'There will be no more death or mourning or crying or pain,' Revelation 21:4, and God Himself is with His people, 21:3. Where the remnant chose Egypt to avoid dying, the final home offers a city that needs no refuge because God's presence is its safety. The people who could not stay in the land will, in Christ, inherit a land they never leave.

quiz.q: What do the remnant's leaders promise Jeremiah before he seeks God's guidance for them?

options.text: That they will obey whatever the LORD says through him, whether the word is pleasant or unpleasant.
options.note: Verses 5 to 6 record this explicit, solemn vow of total obedience in advance of the answer.

options.text: That they will follow his advice only if it matches their own plans.
options.note: Their stated vow is unconditional obedience, though their actions later prove otherwise.

options.text: That they will consult Egyptian officials as well before deciding.
options.note: No mention is made of consulting Egyptian officials; the vow concerns obedience to the LORD's word alone.

options.text: That they will wait one year before acting on his answer.
options.note: They actually wait only ten days for the answer, and act on their rejection of it almost immediately.

quiz.q: What is God's actual answer to the remnant's request for guidance?

options.text: Stay in the land and do not fear Babylon; if they go to Egypt instead, the very sword and famine they fear will overtake them there.
options.note: Verses 10 to 17 give this exact answer, blessing for staying and disaster for fleeing to Egypt.

options.text: Go immediately to Egypt for safety from Babylon.
options.note: God's answer is the opposite, do not go to Egypt.

options.text: Rebuild Jerusalem's walls before making any decision.
options.note: No instruction about rebuilding walls appears in this passage; the choice is simply stay or flee to Egypt.

options.text: Send messengers to negotiate directly with Nebuchadnezzar.
options.note: God's instruction is not to negotiate but simply to remain in the land and trust Him.

quiz.q: How do the remnant's leaders respond to Jeremiah's answer?

options.text: They accuse him of lying and claim Baruch is manipulating him against them, then force the whole remnant to Egypt.
options.note: Verses 2 to 3 and 5 to 7 record this accusation and the forced march to Egypt, including Jeremiah and Baruch themselves.

options.text: They thank him and immediately settle permanently in the land.
options.note: They do the opposite, rejecting his answer and fleeing to Egypt.

options.text: They ask him to seek a second opinion from another prophet.
options.note: No second prophet is consulted; they simply reject Jeremiah's word outright.

options.text: They agree to stay but banish Jeremiah and Baruch from the remnant.
options.note: They do not banish Jeremiah and Baruch; instead they force both of them along to Egypt.

quiz.q: What sign does God give Jeremiah to perform at Tahpanhes in Egypt?

options.text: To bury large stones at the entrance to Pharaoh's palace, symbolizing where Nebuchadnezzar will set his throne when he conquers Egypt.
options.note: Verses 9 to 10 record this specific sign and its meaning.

options.text: To build an altar and offer sacrifices for the remnant's safety.
options.note: No altar or sacrifice is commanded; the sign is burying stones to symbolize Babylon's coming conquest of Egypt.

options.text: To write a letter to Pharaoh warning him personally.
options.note: No letter to Pharaoh is described; the sign is a symbolic act performed in the sight of the Jewish exiles.

options.text: To fast for forty days in mourning for Jerusalem.
options.note: No fast is commanded here; the specific instruction is the symbolic burial of stones at the palace entrance.

quiz.q: What does Jeremiah say about the sincerity of the remnant's original request for guidance?

options.text: That they deceived themselves, since they had already resolved not to obey before they ever asked.
options.note: Verse 20 states plainly, you have deceived yourselves, exposing the vow's insincerity.

options.text: That their request was entirely sincere and they simply changed their minds afterward.
options.note: Jeremiah's own assessment is self-deception from the outset, not a later, honest change of mind.

options.text: That only Johanan, not the rest of the people, was insincere.
options.note: The charge of self-deception is leveled at the remnant as a whole, not singled out to Johanan alone.

options.text: That God had actually changed His answer after the first ten days.
options.note: God's answer does not change; what changes is the people's willingness to accept it once it proves unwelcome.

questions: The remnant vowed obedience before hearing God's answer, then rejected it the moment it was unwelcome. Where might you be asking for God's guidance while already resolved on your own plan?
Jeremiah told the remnant plainly that they had deceived themselves. Where in your own life might comfortable self-deception be standing in for genuine obedience?

The people fled to Egypt to escape war and hunger, only to be told the very things they feared would follow them there. Where are you seeking safety in something other than trust in God's actual word to you?

Jeremiah and Baruch were dragged into Egypt against their will by others' disobedience, yet God still spoke to and used Jeremiah there. How does it encourage you that God remains present and active even in circumstances you did not choose?

God's first answer to the remnant was full of mercy, build you up, plant you, show you compassion, if only they would trust and remain. Where is God currently offering you a hard but hopeful path that unbelief is tempting you to reject?

translationNotes.note: The ten day delay before God's answer came is not explained but may reflect the ordinary pattern of prophetic waiting on the LORD, underscoring that God's guidance was neither instant nor to be presumed upon, yet was still given faithfully.

The accusation that Baruch was inciting Jeremiah reflects an existing suspicion of Baruch recorded earlier in chapter 36 and 45, showing a pattern of blaming the scribe for messages the people simply did not want to hear from the prophet himself.

My servant Nebuchadnezzar echoes the identical title used of him in Jeremiah 27:6, underscoring that Babylon's king remains God's appointed instrument of judgment even against Egypt, the very land the remnant fled to for refuge from him.
